title: Features and labels
objectives: Name the features and the label in a table of examples.

screens.title: Which column is the answer?
screens.prose: These are the ten emails the spam program learned from. It used the link counts and whether each email says “free”.
screens.question: Sort the three columns: two are what the model sees, one is the answer we want.

hints.text: Which column would we like the model to tell us for a new email?
A new email arrives with its links and words, but no one has marked it.
Links and Says “free” are what the model sees; Spam is the answer.

feedback.correct: Links and “free” go in; Spam is the answer.
feedback.generic: Not quite. For a new email, which column is missing?

byKey.spam: You put Spam where the model looks. A new email comes unmarked, so spam or not is what we want out.
byKey.links: You made Links the answer. A new email shows its links at once; the unknown is whether it is spam.
byKey.free: You made “free” the answer. We can see the words of a new email; spam or not is the unknown.

explain.text: The model sees what a new email shows: its links and its words. It must say the one thing nobody has marked yet: spam or not.

screens.title: Features, labels, examples
screens.prose: The columns the model sees are **features**. The answer we want is the **label**. One row, its features with its label, is one **training example**.
screens.question: How many training examples does this table hold?

hints.text: An example is a row, not a column.
Count the emails.
There are ten rows, one per email.

feedback.correct: Ten rows, so ten training examples.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count rows, not columns.

byKey.columns: You counted the three data columns. An example is a whole row: one email.
byKey.features: Two is the number of features. Each of the ten rows is one example.
byKey.spam-rows: You counted only the spam emails. The not-spam rows are examples too.

explain.text: Each email is one example: two features and a label. There are 10 emails, so 10 examples.

screens.title: House prices
screens.prose: An estate agent wants a model that prices a house before it is sold.
screens.question: Which column is the label?

options.why: The agent knows the bedrooms of a house before it sells. That is a feature.
The garden can be measured at once, so it is a feature.
Distance to the station is known in advance: a feature.

hints.text: Which column does the agent not know for a new house?
The sale price comes last, so it is the label.

feedback.correct: The sale price is what the model must say.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the column that is unknown for a house not yet sold.

explain.text: Bedrooms, garden and distance are known for any house. The price is the unknown the agent wants. So Sold for is the label.

screens.title: Count the features
screens.prose: A college wants to predict who passes the final exam, using what it knows by the spring.
screens.question: How many features does this table give the model?

hints.text: Which column is the label?
Passed? is the answer we want.
The other three columns are features.

feedback.correct: Three features: hours, mock score and classes missed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave out the label and count the rest.

byKey.all: You counted Passed? too. That is the label, not a feature.
byKey.rows: Five is the number of students, the examples.

explain.text: Passed? is the label. Hours revised, mock score and classes missed are what the model sees: 3 features.

screens.title: The label in disguise
screens.prose: A phone company wants to spot customers who will complain, early enough to help them first.
screens.question: Which column should not be used as a feature?

options.why: Calls come before a complaint and can warn of one. That is a fair feature.
This is known in advance and says nothing that comes after a complaint.

hints.text: Which column only becomes yes after something has happened?
Refunds are given in answer to complaints.
Refund issued is the label again, dressed as a feature.

feedback.correct: Refunds follow complaints, so that column gives the answer away.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for a column that is a result of complaining.

byKey.calls: You dropped the helpline calls. They happen before a complaint, so they are a fair early warning.

explain.text: A refund is issued because someone complained, so the column almost repeats the label. A model would lean on it and be useless for spotting complaints early.

screens.title: Known too late
screens.prose: At 9 am a trader wants a model that says whether a share will close above today's opening price.
screens.question: Which columns can the model use at 9 am?

options.text: Yesterday's move and the opening price
All three columns: more data is better
options.why: The closing price is only known at 4.30 pm. A model trained with it looks brilliant and cannot be used at 9 am.

options.text: Only the closing price, the best clue
options.why: The closing price nearly is the answer, and it does not exist yet at 9 am.
Yesterday's move and today's opening price are both known by 9 am.

hints.text: Which of these numbers exist at 9 am?
The closing price is set when the market shuts.
Use only what is known when the prediction is made.

feedback.correct: Only what is known at 9 am can be a feature.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask when each number becomes known.

byKey.all: You used every column. The closing price is a leak: it comes after the moment of prediction.
byKey.close: You picked the closing price. It is a leak: compare it with the opening price and you have the label.

explain.text: A feature must be known when the model is asked. The closing price arrives at 4.30 pm and gives the label away. Using it is called a **leak**.

screens.title: No label at all
screens.prose: A gym wants to group its customers into a few kinds, to plan its classes. Nobody has marked any customer with a kind.
screens.question: What is the label in this table?

options.text: There is none: this is learning without labels
Spend a month, the money column
options.why: Spend is something we know about every customer, so it is a feature.

options.text: Months with us, the loyalty column
options.why: This is known for every customer: a feature, not an answer.
That column only numbers the rows.

hints.text: Is any column the answer someone marked?
No column holds a marked answer; the groups are to be found.

feedback.correct: No label: the model must find groups on its own.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether any column was marked by a person as the answer.

explain.text: Every column here is a feature. With no label, a model can still group similar rows, which is called learning without labels. This course works with labels.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose: Every table so far has the same shape. $$\text{example} = (\text{features},\ \text{label}), \qquad \text{model: features} \to \text{label}$$ Features must be known when the model is asked; the label is what it must say.
screens.question: A table has 200 rows and 6 columns, one of which is the label. How many features does each example have?

hints.text: One of the six columns is not a feature.

feedback.correct: Six columns less the label: 5 features.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the label away from the columns.

byKey.six: You counted the label as a feature. Five columns remain once it is set aside.
byKey.rows: 200 is the number of examples. Features are columns.

explain.text: One column is the label, so $6 - 1 = 5$ columns are features. The 200 rows are the examples.

screens.title: Tomorrow's sign
screens.prose: A quant builds a dataset of daily returns. The label is whether the share rises tomorrow. A colleague adds tomorrow's volume as a feature.
screens.question: Why can tomorrow's volume not be a feature?

options.text: It is not known when the prediction is made, tonight
Volume numbers are too big to use
options.why: Size does not matter; any number can be a feature. Timing does.

options.text: Volume never tells us anything about returns
options.why: It may well carry information. The trouble is that tomorrow's is not known tonight.
The label is tomorrow up or not. Volume is a different column, but one from the future.

hints.text: When would the model be run?
Tonight, before tomorrow trades.
Tomorrow's volume does not exist yet, so it is a leak.

feedback.correct: Tomorrow's volume is a leak: it arrives with the answer.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask when each column becomes known.

byKey.weak: You judged its usefulness. Even a useful column is barred if it is only known after the prediction.

explain.text: The model must run tonight using today's return and today's volume. Tomorrow's volume is known only when tomorrow is over, with the label. A backtest that uses it looks good and cannot be traded.

ideas: Features are what the model sees; the label is the answer we want it to give.
One row, its features with its label, is one training example.
A feature must be known when the model is asked; a column that arrives later is a leak.

formula.name: An example
formula.note: Features are known in advance; the label is the unknown.

summary.trap: A column that is only known after the event, such as the closing price, gives the label away.

quiz.prose: A bank's table of past loans has: income, loan size, years at address, and repaid or not.
quiz.question: Which is the label for a model that decides on new loans?

options.why: Income is known when someone applies, so it is a feature.
The loan size is known at the start: a feature.

feedback.correct: Repaid or not is what the bank wants to know in advance.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which column is unknown for a new applicant?

explain.text: A new applicant shows income, loan size and address. Whether they repay is the unknown. That is the label.

quiz.prose: A table holds 48 days of a share, with 7 columns: 6 numbers known each evening and whether the share rose the next day.
quiz.question: How many training examples are there?

feedback.correct: Each day is a row: 48 examples.
feedback.generic: Not quite. An example is a row.

byKey.cols: 7 is the number of columns. Each of the 48 days is an example.
byKey.features: 6 is the number of features. Count the rows.

explain.text: One row per day, so 48 examples. Each has 6 features and a label.

quiz.prose: A shop predicts each morning whether a customer will buy today. Columns: visits last week, items in basket at closing time, minutes on the website yesterday.
quiz.question: Which column is a leak?

options.text: Items in basket at closing time

options.why: Last week's visits are known each morning. Fair feature.
Yesterday is over by the morning, so this is known in time.

feedback.correct: The closing basket is only known after the day.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which number arrives after the morning?

explain.text: At closing time the day is over, so the basket nearly tells you whether they bought. It is not known in the morning, so it is a leak.
